newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK MINISTER SEES DRAMATIC FALL IN INFLATION.
newsitem.headline: GREEK MINISTER SEES DRAMATIC FALL IN INFLATION.

text.p: Inflation will fall dramatically in the first half of 1997, allowing the Greek government to fully implement its toughest budget in 15 years, Interior and Public Administration Minister Alekos Papadopoulos said.

"In 1997 and particularly the first half year there will be a dramatic fall in inflation... the budget will be implemented .. but it demands self-discipline and self-restraint from the whole of Greek society," he told financial daily "Express".
Lower inflation, Papadopoulos said, was crucial for Greece's future in the European Union.

"Greece is debt-ridden. This year the debt is close to 36 trillion drahmas and almost 100 percent of tax revenues will go on interest payments... for these expenses to be reduced and for there to be a surplus which will allow the government to practice development and social policies, interest rates must fall. For these to fall, inflation must fall... If this does not happen, our course towards convergence will be very difficult if not impossible," he said.
Papadopoulos, socialist finance minister from 1993 to 1996, said he was not worried about the budget -- dubbed the toughest in 15 years -- causing social unrest.

"Portugal, Spain and France, and now Italy, implemented far more austere stability programmes, more austere than ours, and did not cause social unrest. It is an issue of maintaining a balance on the social level," he said.

He warned against seeing European unification as a panacea for all the country's ills and said the impressive in fall in inflation and interest rates and increased revenues in the past three years did not mean the economy was out of the woods.
"The country's problems will be solved by the increase in production and productivity," he said. "We must continue the efforts to fiscal discipline and adjustment."

"There is only one road: for us to organise a strong economy and a more flexible and effective state. Otherwise we will not be able to deal with European competition," he said. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
